docs.text: Business case previews ¶ Five business problems, one for each department. Each case teaches a core skill and a common mistake to catch. Previews, not assignments yet These are proposed case themes. Individual files have not been released yet. We combine selected Tableau sample datasets with synthetic (made-up) teaching data. Meridian Commerce is a proposed fictional company used only for the synthetic cases. Real datasets keep their own context, units and dates. The five core cases ¶ Retail ¶ Decision: Which customer segment deserves a closer investigation? You will practise: what a row means, distinct orders, average order value, Sales and Profit, ratios, discounts, customers, trends and the limits of a returns list. Mistake to catch: treating order lines as orders. Finance ¶ Decision: Which departments need a spending review? You will practise: budget versus actual, time periods, reconciliation and whether a cost difference is favourable. Mistake to catch: repeating a monthly budget on every transaction row. Operations ¶ Decision: Where should delivery reliability improve? You will practise: promised dates, overdue open shipments, distributions, median and mean. Mistake to catch: dropping undelivered shipments from the service measure. Marketing ¶ Decision: Which campaigns need closer evaluation before budget moves? You will practise: weighted funnel rates, cost per conversion, return on ad spend and the limits of attribution. Mistake to catch: averaging percentages that have different denominators. HR ¶ Decision: How is the workforce changing, and which comparisons are fair? You will practise: historical headcount, turnover, cohorts, tenure and recruitment timelines. All employee records are synthetic. Mistake to catch: dividing past exits by the current headcount. docs.text: From business question to recommendation ¶ A useful analysis supports a decision. A chart becomes trustworthy when its population, calculations and limitations are clear. We follow the same seven steps in every lesson and case. The seven steps ¶ 1. Business question ¶ Ask: Who must decide what, and by when? Keep: the decision and a one-sentence question. 2. Data understanding ¶ Ask: What does each row represent? What is missing? Keep: the grain, keys, units, data dictionary and scope. 3. Preparation ¶ Ask: What changes are needed, and could someone else repeat them? Keep: an untouched copy of the original data and a log of every change. 4. Analysis ¶ Ask: Which comparison or metric actually answers the question? Keep: the metric definition, filters and calculation. 5. Validation ¶ Ask: Do totals reconcile? Can I explain any odd values? Keep: a manual spot check, count and total checks, and edge cases. 6. Visualization ¶ Ask: Can the audience see the important comparison at a glance? Keep: a labelled chart showing the period, units and population. 7. Recommendation ¶ Ask: What action follows, and what is still uncertain? Keep: an action linked to evidence, one caveat and a follow-up measure. A worked example ¶ Why are orders falling? A manager asks: "Why are orders falling?" The data file has one row per order line , so a single order with three products takes up three rows. Counting rows would count lines , not orders. First, define what an order is, which period to look at and which orders are eligible. Then count distinct order IDs in that population. Compare the result with an order-level summary before reading anything into the trend. The same care applies elsewhere in the course: a budget repeated on every row after a join undelivered shipments left out of a service calculation campaign percentages averaged without their volumes past staff exits divided by today's headcount When a result looks wrong ¶ Work through these checks in order: Grain and keys Date filters Missing values Join or relationship behaviour Aggregation Then write down why the wrong answer was tempting and what evidence supports the corrected one. A plausible number is not a checked number Looking reasonable is not the same as being validated. Association is not causation ¶ A pattern in the data can tell you where to look . It does not prove that a discount, campaign, carrier or HR policy caused a result. When a decision depends on cause and effect, recommend a follow-up comparison or a test.

docs.text: Why data analytics matters ¶ Every organisation makes decisions. Data analytics is the discipline of making those decisions with evidence instead of guesswork, and of explaining that evidence so other people act on it. Before we open Tableau, this Foundations section answers a simple question: why bother? You will see how analysis has changed real outcomes, how numbers can mislead, and why the way we present evidence matters as much as the evidence itself. What is data analytics? ¶ Data analytics turns raw records into answers to business questions. It usually works at four levels: Level Question it answers Everyday example Descriptive What happened? Sales fell 8% last quarter. Diagnostic Why did it happen? The fall came almost entirely from one region after a competitor opened. Predictive What is likely to happen next? If nothing changes, the region will lose a further 5% next quarter. Prescriptive What should we do about it? Test a local loyalty offer in that region before changing national prices. This course focuses mostly on the first two levels, done properly : a clear question, trustworthy data, correct calculations, honest charts and a recommendation a manager can act on. Real stories where data changed the outcome ¶ A map that changed how we think about disease (London, 1854) ¶ During a cholera outbreak in Soho, physician John Snow investigated where the victims lived and where they drew their water. The cases clustered around one public water pump on Broad Street. At the time, most experts blamed "bad air". Snow persuaded the local authorities to remove the pump's handle. His famous dot map of the deaths, drawn shortly afterwards, became the classic demonstration that cholera spreads through water, though it took years for that view to be widely accepted. Lesson A simple, well-chosen picture of the data can overturn what "everyone knows". A chart that reformed hospitals (1850s) ¶ After the Crimean War, Florence Nightingale showed with her "rose" diagrams that far more soldiers died of preventable disease in hospitals than of battle wounds. Her charts were designed for politicians, not statisticians, and helped drive major sanitary reforms. Lesson Analysis only changes things when the people who decide can understand it. Winning on a small budget (baseball, 2002) ¶ The Oakland Athletics , with one of the lowest payrolls in Major League Baseball, used statistics such as on-base percentage to find undervalued players. They competed with teams spending far more. The story became the book and film Moneyball , and data-driven scouting spread across sport. Lesson Measuring the right thing can matter more than having the most money. Preparing for a hurricane (retail, 2004) ¶ Before a hurricane reached Florida, Walmart analysts looked at what shoppers had bought before earlier storms. Alongside torches and water, sales of strawberry Pop-Tarts and beer reportedly jumped well above normal. Stores were stocked accordingly. Lesson Past patterns can guide practical, everyday operational decisions. When big data got it wrong (public health, 2008–2015) ¶ Google Flu Trends tried to estimate flu levels from search queries. It worked for a while, then missed the 2009 swine-flu pandemic and badly overestimated later flu seasons, and was shut down. People's search habits and Google's own search algorithms changed, and the model was not re-checked against official flu data often enough. Lesson More data is not automatically better data. Every result still needs validation. Where you meet analytics every day ¶ Banking: a card payment is flagged as possible fraud because it does not fit your normal pattern. Streaming and shopping: recommendations are based on what similar customers watched or bought. Transport: ride-hailing prices rise when demand outstrips available drivers. Healthcare: hospitals plan staff rotas using predicted admission levels. Workplaces: HR teams track hiring time and staff turnover to spot problems early. Why presentation is part of analysis ¶ An analysis that nobody understands has no effect. The most important finding in a report can be lost in a cluttered table, a misleading chart or a slide with too much text. Good analysts therefore do three jobs: Find what is true in the data. Check that it really is true. Show it so the right person understands it quickly and acts on it. The rest of this Foundations section covers each of these. What comes next ¶ Work through these pages in order: Statistics are not enough : why you must always look at the data, not just the summary numbers. How statistics can mislead : correlation versus causation, misleading charts and other traps. Types of analysis : looking at one, two or many variables at once. Designing clear visuals : data-ink, how the eye groups things, and using colour with purpose. Storytelling with data : the Challenger disaster, and how to turn analysis into a message people act on. Try this before moving on Think of one decision at your own workplace that was made on gut feeling. Write down: what data could have informed it, who would have needed to understand that data, what could have gone wrong if the data had been misread.

Real stories where data changed the outcome

docs.text: During a cholera outbreak in Soho, physician John Snow investigated where the victims lived and where they drew their water. The cases clustered around one public water pump on Broad Street. At the time, most experts blamed "bad air". Snow persuaded the local authorities to remove the pump's handle. His famous dot map of the deaths, drawn shortly afterwards, became the classic demonstration that cholera spreads through water, though it took years for that view to be widely accepted. Lesson A simple, well-chosen picture of the data can overturn what "everyone knows".
docs.title: A map that changed how we think about disease (London, 1854)

docs.text: After the Crimean War, Florence Nightingale showed with her "rose" diagrams that far more soldiers died of preventable disease in hospitals than of battle wounds. Her charts were designed for politicians, not statisticians, and helped drive major sanitary reforms. Lesson Analysis only changes things when the people who decide can understand it.
docs.title: A chart that reformed hospitals (1850s)

docs.text: The Oakland Athletics , with one of the lowest payrolls in Major League Baseball, used statistics such as on-base percentage to find undervalued players. They competed with teams spending far more. The story became the book and film Moneyball , and data-driven scouting spread across sport. Lesson Measuring the right thing can matter more than having the most money.
docs.title: Winning on a small budget (baseball, 2002)

docs.text: Before a hurricane reached Florida, Walmart analysts looked at what shoppers had bought before earlier storms. Alongside torches and water, sales of strawberry Pop-Tarts and beer reportedly jumped well above normal. Stores were stocked accordingly. Lesson Past patterns can guide practical, everyday operational decisions.
docs.title: Preparing for a hurricane (retail, 2004)

docs.text: Google Flu Trends tried to estimate flu levels from search queries. It worked for a while, then missed the 2009 swine-flu pandemic and badly overestimated later flu seasons, and was shut down. People's search habits and Google's own search algorithms changed, and the model was not re-checked against official flu data often enough. Lesson More data is not automatically better data. Every result still needs validation.
docs.title: When big data got it wrong (public health, 2008–2015)

docs.text: Banking: a card payment is flagged as possible fraud because it does not fit your normal pattern. Streaming and shopping: recommendations are based on what similar customers watched or bought. Transport: ride-hailing prices rise when demand outstrips available drivers. Healthcare: hospitals plan staff rotas using predicted admission levels. Workplaces: HR teams track hiring time and staff turnover to spot problems early.

docs.text: An analysis that nobody understands has no effect. The most important finding in a report can be lost in a cluttered table, a misleading chart or a slide with too much text. Good analysts therefore do three jobs: Find what is true in the data. Check that it really is true. Show it so the right person understands it quickly and acts on it. The rest of this Foundations section covers each of these.

docs.text: How statistics can mislead ¶ Numbers feel objective, but the same data can support very different stories depending on how it is summarised, compared and drawn. Learn the common traps so you never fall into them, and can spot them in other people's work. In 1954, Darrell Huff wrote a short, famous book called How to Lie with Statistics . Its point was not to teach lying. It was to show readers how easily numbers mislead, often by accident. The traps below are the ones you will meet most often at work. 1. Correlation is not causation ¶ Two things that move together are correlated . That does not mean one causes the other. A classic example: in many cities, ice cream sales and crime both rise in summer and fall in winter. Plot one against the other and you see a strong relationship. Does ice cream cause crime? Of course not. Both are plausibly driven by a third factor, warm weather , when more people are outside. The chart uses synthetic data made up for illustration. The hidden third factor is called a confounder . Whenever you see two things moving together, ask: Could a third factor be driving both? Could the cause run the other way? Could it be coincidence, especially if I searched through many variables? Spurious correlations If you compare enough unrelated series, some will match by pure chance. Tyler Vigen's Spurious Correlations project collects amusing examples, such as films featuring a particular actor tracking the number of swimming-pool drownings in the same years. At work "Customers who used our app spent 30% more." Perhaps the app made them spend more. Or perhaps the customers who already spent the most were the ones who bothered to download the app. Only a fair comparison or a test can tell you which. 2. Simpson's paradox: the total can reverse the parts ¶ In 1973, the University of California, Berkeley, looked at graduate admissions. Overall, 44% of men but only 35% of women were admitted. It looked like clear bias against women. But when the figures were split by department, the picture changed. The chart and table show the six largest departments; the overall row covers all departments. Department Men admitted Women admitted A 62% 82% B 63% 68% C 37% 34% D 33% 35% E 28% 24% F 6% 7% All departments (overall) 44% 35% What happened? Women applied mostly to departments that were very competitive for everyone (C to F). Men applied mostly to departments that admitted many applicants (A and B). The overall rate mixed together very different groups. The lesson Before comparing two overall rates, check whether the groups being compared have a different mix underneath. A total can tell the opposite story to every one of its parts. 3. Misleading axes ¶ The same two numbers can look dramatically different depending on where the axis starts. Synthetic data for illustration. Bar charts should start at zero, because we judge bars by their length. Line charts may start elsewhere, because we judge lines by their slope, but label the axis clearly. Watch for two different y-axes on one chart. They let the author make any two lines appear to move together. 4. Cherry-picked time windows ¶ Choose the start and end dates carefully and almost any trend can be made to look like growth or decline. "Sales up 40% since March!" (March was the worst month in five years.) "Complaints halved this quarter!" (Last quarter included a one-off system outage.) Synthetic data for illustration. The left chart is true, but the right chart shows the real story: March was an unusual low, and sales have been falling for five years. Ask Why does the chart start and end there ? What does the longer history look like? 5. Which average? ¶ The word "average" can mean different things: The mean adds everything up and divides by the count. The median is the middle value when everything is sorted. If a few values are extremely large, the mean is pulled upward. Imagine nine employees earning 40,000 and one director earning 1,000,000. The mean salary is 136,000; the median is 40,000. Both are "the average salary", but only one describes a typical employee. Synthetic data for illustration. Which to use Use the median for things with a few very large values, such as salaries, house prices or delivery delays. Report both when the difference matters. 6. Percentages without the base ¶ "Complaints rose 200%!" sounds alarming. From 1 to 3, it is not. From 10,000 to 30,000, it is a crisis. Synthetic data for illustration. Notice that the two charts look exactly the same. Only the axis numbers reveal how different the situations are. Always ask for the count behind a percentage. Be wary of averaging percentages from groups of very different sizes. You will meet this trap in the marketing case. 7. Survivorship bias ¶ As the story is usually told, during the Second World War analysts studied bombers returning from missions and mapped where they had been hit. The obvious idea was to add armour where the bullet holes were. The statistician Abraham Wald pointed out the flaw: these were the planes that survived . Planes hit in other places, such as the engines, never came back to be counted. The armour belonged where the returning planes had no holes. Simplified illustration, not real wartime data. At work Surveying only current customers about why they like you tells you nothing about why others left. Studying only successful projects hides the reasons projects fail. A checklist for any number you are shown ¶ Before you trust a figure, ask: Compared to what? A number without a comparison means little. Who or what is included? Which records, which dates, which filters? What is the denominator? Out of how many? Could something else explain it? A confounder, a different mix, chance? How is it drawn? Where does the axis start? Is the time window fair? Try it yourself ¶ Exercise 1: name the confounder For each claim, suggest a third factor that could explain the link: Towns with more fire engines have more fire damage. Employees who attend more training get promoted more often. Stores with more staff have more customer complaints. Exercise 2: fix the chart Find a chart in a news article or a company report. Check where its axis starts, which time period it covers and whether the counts behind its percentages are shown. Rewrite its headline so it is fair. Exercise 3: spot the paradox A sales manager says: "Team A's overall conversion rate is lower than Team B's, so Team A is weaker." What extra breakdown would you ask for before agreeing?

docs.text: Statistics are not enough ¶ Averages, spreads and correlations are useful summaries. But very different data can produce exactly the same summary numbers. The only safe habit is to look at the data as well. Anscombe's quartet ¶ In 1973 the statistician Francis Anscombe created four small datasets. Each has eleven points. Look at their summary statistics: Statistic Dataset I Dataset II Dataset III Dataset IV Mean of x 9.0 9.0 9.0 9.0 Mean of y 7.50 7.50 7.50 7.50 Variance of x 11.0 11.0 11.0 11.0 Variance of y 4.13 4.13 4.12 4.12 Correlation of x and y 0.816 0.816 0.816 0.817 Best-fit line y = 3.00 + 0.500x y = 3.00 + 0.500x y = 3.00 + 0.500x y = 3.00 + 0.500x If you only read this table, you would say the four datasets are the same. Now look at them: Dataset What the picture shows What the statistics hide I A loose, roughly straight-line relationship Nothing. This is the case the summary describes well. II A smooth curve The relationship is not a straight line at all. III A perfect straight line, except for one outlier A single unusual point drags the trend line. IV Almost all points share one x value; one extreme point creates the "trend" Remove that one point and every x is the same, so there is no trend left to measure. The lesson Summary statistics compress data. Compression throws information away. A chart lets you see what was thrown away. The raw data, if you want to plot it yourself x (I, II, III) y I y II y III x IV y IV 10 8.04 9.14 7.46 8 6.58 8 6.95 8.14 6.77 8 5.76 13 7.58 8.74 12.74 8 7.71 9 8.81 8.77 7.11 8 8.84 11 8.33 9.26 7.81 8 8.47 14 9.96 8.10 8.84 8 7.04 6 7.24 6.13 6.08 8 5.25 4 4.26 3.10 5.39 19 12.50 12 10.84 9.13 8.15 8 5.56 7 4.82 7.26 6.42 8 7.91 5 5.68 4.74 5.73 8 6.89 The Datasaurus Dozen ¶ In 2017, researchers Justin Matejka and George Fitzmaurice took the idea further. Starting from a dinosaur drawing made of data points (originally created by Alberto Cairo), they nudged points step by step into new shapes while keeping the summary statistics nearly identical, to about two decimal places. Every one of these thirteen datasets has: mean of x ≈ 54.3 and mean of y ≈ 47.8 standard deviation of x ≈ 16.8 and of y ≈ 26.9 correlation between x and y between −0.06 and −0.07 A report that said "x and y are essentially unrelated, centred around 54 and 48" would be technically correct for all of them, including the dinosaur. Data source Datasaurus Dozen data from the open-source datasauRus package (MIT licence), based on Matejka and Fitzmaurice, Same Stats, Different Graphs , ACM CHI 2017. What this means at work ¶ You will rarely meet a dinosaur in a sales report. But you will meet the same problems in everyday forms: An average hides two very different groups. Average delivery time looks fine, because most deliveries are fast while a few customers wait weeks. One outlier drives the trend. A single huge order makes a quiet month look like growth. A relationship is curved, not straight. Discounts raise sales up to a point, then only cut profit. Rule of thumb Never report a summary number you have not also looked at in a chart, at least once, yourself. Try it yourself ¶ Exercise 1: predict, then check Cover the Anscombe chart above. Using only the statistics table, sketch what you think each dataset looks like. Then uncover the chart. Which of your sketches was furthest off, and why? Exercise 2: find a hidden shape at work Think of a number you see regularly in your job, for example average monthly sales or average response time. Write down two different situations that would produce the same average but would need different decisions . Exercise 3: in Tableau (after Lesson 1) Type the Anscombe data from the table above into a spreadsheet with three columns: dataset (I, II, III or IV), x and y , one row per point (44 rows). Connect Tableau to it, then: Drag dataset to Columns , then drag x to Columns to its right. Drag y to Rows . Open the Analysis menu and untick Aggregate Measures , so each row becomes its own point instead of one summed mark per dataset. You have just recreated the quartet.

docs.text: Storytelling with data ¶ A correct analysis that nobody understands changes nothing. Storytelling with data means shaping evidence into a clear message, for a specific audience, that leads to a decision. The Challenger disaster: right data, wrong presentation ¶ On 28 January 1986 , the space shuttle Challenger broke apart 73 seconds after launch, killing all seven crew. The investigation found that rubber O-ring seals in a booster rocket had failed. They had become stiff in the unusually cold weather: the air temperature at launch was about 36°F (2°C) , far colder than any previous launch. The night before, engineers at the contractor Morton Thiokol were worried. They had data on O-ring damage from earlier flights and recommended not launching below 53°F, the coldest temperature previously flown. In a tense teleconference, their recommendation was challenged, managers reversed it, and the launch went ahead. What did the data show? ¶ Discussion that night focused on flights where O-rings had been damaged , the view later highlighted by the Rogers Commission investigation. Looked at alone, those flights do not show an obvious temperature pattern: damage appeared at both cool and warm temperatures. The picture changes completely when you include the flights with no damage: What you see Only damaged flights All 23 flights Pattern with temperature Unclear Every flight below 65°F had O-ring damage Launches near 36°F None None. Challenger was far outside all experience Every launch below 65°F had damage. Most warm launches had none. And Challenger would launch more than 15 degrees colder than anything ever tried. Two views of the lesson Edward Tufte argued in Visual Explanations (1997) that the engineers' charts failed to show this relationship clearly. Others have pointed out that the engineers did raise temperature as the key concern, and that the decision was also shaped by schedule and organisational pressure. Both views lead to the same lesson for analysts: when the stakes are high, the evidence must be presented so the risk is impossible to miss. Data source O-ring data for the 23 flights before Challenger: UCI Machine Learning Repository, Challenger USA Space Shuttle O-Ring dataset (erosion or blow-by version), based on Draper (1995) and Dalal, Fowlkes and Hoadley (1989). What makes a data story ¶ The ideas in this section draw on Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic's book Storytelling with Data (2015), paraphrased for this course. A data story is not a decorated chart. It has three parts: Context: who is the audience, what do they already know, and what decision do they face? Evidence: the few charts and numbers that matter, checked and clearly drawn. Action: what you recommend, what is uncertain, and how success will be measured. Start with the "big idea" ¶ Before building any chart, write your main message in one sentence that: states your point of view, says what is at stake, and is written for your audience. Example: "Delivery delays in the North region are costing us repeat customers, so we should trial a second carrier there next quarter before the peak season." If you cannot write that sentence, you are not ready to build the presentation. A simple process ¶ Know your audience. A finance director and a warehouse team need different levels of detail. Write the big idea in one sentence. Choose the right chart for each point (see Types of analysis ). Remove clutter (see Designing clear visuals ). Direct attention with one colour, a clear title and a short annotation. Build the flow: situation, complication, resolution. What is happening, why it is a problem, what we should do. Test it on someone who has not seen it. Can they repeat your message in one sentence? Titles that tell Replace descriptive titles with message titles. Instead of "Monthly sales by region" write "North region sales have fallen for three months while all others grew." Exploratory versus explanatory ¶ Exploratory Explanatory Purpose Find out what is in the data Tell others what you found Audience You Decision-makers Number of charts Many As few as possible Style Rough, quick Clean, titled, annotated Most of your time in analysis is exploratory. Only the few findings that matter make it into the explanatory story. Try it yourself ¶ Exercise 1: rescue the Challenger chart Look at the left-hand Challenger chart. Write a one-sentence title for the right-hand chart that a manager could not misunderstand. Exercise 2: write a big idea Choose a recent finding from your own work, or from any chart on these Foundations pages. Write a big-idea sentence with a point of view, the stakes and the audience. Exercise 3: three slides, one story Plan a three-slide story about the ice cream and crime example on How statistics can mislead : Situation: what the raw correlation seems to say. Complication: what it hides. Resolution: what a decision-maker should do instead. Exercise 4: the one-sentence test Show any chart you have made to a colleague for ten seconds. Ask them what it says. If their answer differs from your intended message, revise the title, the highlight or the chart type.

Example: "Delivery delays in the North region are costing us repeat customers, so we should trial a second carrier there next quarter before the peak season." If you cannot write that sentence, you are not ready to build the presentation.

docs.text: Know your audience. A finance director and a warehouse team need different levels of detail. Write the big idea in one sentence. Choose the right chart for each point (see Types of analysis ). Remove clutter (see Designing clear visuals ). Direct attention with one colour, a clear title and a short annotation. Build the flow: situation, complication, resolution. What is happening, why it is a problem, what we should do. Test it on someone who has not seen it. Can they repeat your message in one sentence? Titles that tell Replace descriptive titles with message titles. Instead of "Monthly sales by region" write "North region sales have fallen for three months while all others grew."

docs.text: Types of analysis: one, two or many variables ¶ Most questions start with one variable, then ask how it relates to a second, and finally how several factors work together. Each step needs different summaries and different charts. Synthetic data for illustration. Univariate analysis: one variable at a time ¶ Question: What does this one variable look like? You describe its centre (mean, median), spread (range, standard deviation) and shape (symmetric, skewed, any outliers). Kind of variable Good summaries Good charts Numbers (sales, days, age) Mean, median, minimum, maximum, spread Histogram, box plot Categories (region, product type) Counts and percentages Bar chart sorted by size Dates Counts per day, week or month Line chart over time Business examples: How long do deliveries usually take, and how long do the slowest ones take? Which product category sells most often? How many customer complaints arrive each week? Watch for A skewed shape. In the histogram above, most orders arrive within 1 to 5 days, but a long tail stretches past two weeks. The median (3 days) describes a typical order better than the mean (about 4 days), which the slow tail pulls upward. Bivariate analysis: two variables together ¶ Question: How does one variable change with another? The two variables are… Good summaries Good charts Number and number Correlation, trend line Scatter plot Category and number Mean or median per group Bar chart, box plot per group Category and category Counts in a cross-table Heat map, stacked or grouped bar Date and number Change over time Line chart Business examples: Does higher advertising spend go with higher revenue? Do some regions have longer delivery times than others? Which customer segments buy which product categories? Remember A relationship between two variables is a correlation , not proof of cause. See How statistics can mislead . Multivariate analysis: three or more variables ¶ Question: Does the relationship change when we account for something else? You add a third variable by using colour , size , small multiples (one small chart per group) or filters . Business examples: Does the link between ad spend and revenue differ by sales channel? Do delivery times by region change once we separate standard and express shipping? Is a profit drop explained by a change in the product mix? The second and third panels show exactly the same points. Colouring by channel in the third panel shows that "Store" tends to sit above the others at the same spend, on average. That pattern is invisible in the two-variable chart. Rule of thumb Add one variable at a time. If a chart needs a long explanation, split it into small multiples instead. Choosing a chart: quick guide ¶ I want to show… Try How values are distributed Histogram or box plot A ranking Sorted bar chart Change over time Line chart Parts of a whole (few parts) Stacked bar; a pie only for two or three slices Relationship between two numbers Scatter plot Comparison across many groups Small multiples or a heat map A single headline number Just the number, large and clearly labelled Try it yourself ¶ Exercise 1: classify the question Is each question univariate, bivariate or multivariate? What is the typical order value? Do larger discounts go with lower profit? Does the discount–profit relationship differ between furniture and office supplies? How many orders were placed each month? Exercise 2: pick the chart For each question in Exercise 1, choose a chart type from the quick guide and say in one sentence why. Exercise 3: your own data Pick one variable from your own work. Write one univariate, one bivariate and one multivariate question you could ask about it.

docs.text: Designing clear visuals ¶ A good chart lets the reader see the important comparison in seconds. That depends on removing what does not help, and on using what we know about how the eye and brain read pictures. The data-ink ratio ¶ Information designer Edward Tufte suggested a simple test. Of all the ink on a chart, how much actually shows data ? Everything else (heavy gridlines, borders, shading, 3D effects, decorative colours) is non-data ink. Tufte called unnecessary decoration chartjunk . Aim: increase the share of ink that carries data, without removing anything the reader needs. Synthetic data for illustration. What changed between the two versions: Removed the background shading, borders and hatching. Removed the gridlines and the value axis, and wrote the values directly on the bars. Sorted the bars, so the ranking is obvious. Used colour once , to point at the bar that matters. Turned the bars horizontal , so labels are easy to read. Do not overdo it Removing axis labels, units or context to make a chart "clean" makes it less useful. The goal is clarity, not minimalism. Pre-attentive attributes: what the eye sees first ¶ Some visual differences are noticed almost instantly, before we consciously think. These are called pre-attentive attributes . They include colour, size, position, orientation and boldness. Try it: count the number 3 in the top grid, then in the bottom grid. The bottom grid takes a second. The top one takes much longer. The only difference is one attribute: colour. Use this deliberately Make most of the chart grey, then use one strong colour or bold label for the thing you want the reader to see. If everything is highlighted, nothing is. Gestalt principles: how we group things ¶ Our brains automatically group what we see. Designers use these Gestalt principles to make related items look related. Principle What it means Use it in a chart or dashboard Proximity Things close together seem related Put related charts next to each other; leave space between unrelated ones Similarity Things that look alike (colour, shape) seem related Use the same colour for the same category on every chart Enclosure Things inside a shared border or shaded area seem grouped Shade a time period, such as a promotion, on a line chart Connection Things joined by a line seem related Lines connect points in a time series; avoid lines between unrelated categories Closure We complete incomplete shapes in our minds Charts rarely need full borders; the eye fills them in Continuity We follow smooth paths Align charts and labels so the eye flows across the page Colour with purpose ¶ One colour for one meaning. If "East" is blue in one chart, keep it blue in every chart. Grey for context, colour for focus. Do not rely on colour alone. Around one in twelve men has some colour-vision deficiency. Add labels or patterns too. Avoid rainbow palettes for numbers. Use light-to-dark shades of one colour for "more" and "less". Avoid red and green as the only difference. It is the most common pair people cannot tell apart. A clean-chart checklist ¶ Does the title say what the reader should notice, not just what is plotted? Are axes labelled with units, and do bars start at zero? Is everything that is not data as light as possible? Is colour used only where it means something? Can someone who cannot see colour still read it? Would a sorted table or a single number be clearer than a chart? Try it yourself ¶ Exercise 1: declutter Take a chart from a recent report at work, or any chart from the news. List every element that is not data. For each, decide: keep , lighten or remove . Sketch the improved version. Exercise 2: one highlight Sketch a bar chart of five products where only one product needs attention. Use grey for four bars and one colour for the fifth. Write a title that tells the reader what to notice. Exercise 3: spot the Gestalt Open any dashboard you use at work. Find one place where proximity or similarity helps you, and one place where it confuses you.

docs.text: Lesson 1: From decision to evidence ¶ Turn a vague business request into a clear question, open your first dataset in Tableau, and build a first chart you can explain. Draft lesson The Tableau steps on this page have not yet been rehearsed on the course version of Tableau. Menu names may differ slightly on your computer. Your facilitator will confirm them in class. The business decision ¶ The head of a retail business says: "Sales feel uneven across our customer groups. I need to know where to look first." This is not yet a question you can answer with data. Today you will turn it into one, and then take a first look at the evidence. About the data We use a fictitious retail sample published by Tableau (the "Superstore" sample), prepared for this course. It is not a real company. Sales and Profit are in the file's own monetary units; the currency is not stated, so we never label it as dollars, rupees or anything else. What you will be able to do ¶ By the end of this lesson you will be able to: Write a business question that names a decision, a population and a time period. Connect Tableau to a CSV file and recognise dimensions and measures. Build a simple bar chart and add a filter. Explain the difference between one row and one order in this file. Save your workbook on your computer and reopen it. Evidence you keep: your written question, a saved first chart and a one-sentence explanation of what a row means. Before you start ¶ Read the Foundations pages. They explain why the habits in this lesson matter. Install Tableau Desktop Public Edition (see Setup and practice ). Complete the smoke test: open a CSV, create a sum, save, close and reopen. Get the course file order_lines.csv (release superstore-retail-v1 ) from your facilitator. Save it in a folder you can find again, for example Documents/DataAnalytics/data . If Tableau will not install or open Tell your facilitator before the session. You can follow the demonstration, pair with a classmate and still write your question and notes. You will build your own chart later. Part 1: From request to question ¶ A good analytical question answers four things: Part Ask yourself Example Decision What will someone do differently? Choose one customer segment to investigate next month Population Which records count? All order lines in the course file Period Which dates? Orders placed in 2023, 2024 and 2025 Measure What will we compare? Sales by customer segment Putting it together: "Which customer segment had the highest Sales for orders placed in 2023–2025, so we can choose one segment to investigate next month?" Your turn Rewrite the head's request as your own question. Use the four parts in the table. Keep it to one sentence. Part 2: Watch the demonstration ¶ Your facilitator will connect to the file and build a first chart while you watch. Before each step, predict what you think will happen. Things to notice: How Tableau reads each column (text, number or date). Which fields appear as dimensions (things you group by) and which as measures (numbers you add up). What happens to a number when you drag it into the view. Part 3: Guided practice ¶ Follow along step by step. Connect to the file ¶ Open Tableau Desktop Public Edition. In the Connect pane on the left, under To a File , choose Text file . Find and open order_lines.csv . Tableau opens the Data Source page with a preview of the rows. Check the column types ¶ Look at the small icon above each column in the preview: Icon Meaning Examples in this file Abc Text order_id, segment, region # Number sales, profit, quantity Calendar Date order_date, ship_date Check the IDs order_id and row_id are identifiers, not amounts. Adding them up means nothing. If an ID shows as a number, note it in your log. Tableau may tidy column names for display, for example showing order_id as Order Id . It is the same field. Build a first chart ¶ Click the Sheet 1 tab at the bottom. In the Data pane, find Segment and drag it to Rows . Find Sales and drag it to Columns . You should see one bar per segment. Tableau shows this as SUM(Sales) . Add a filter ¶ Drag Region to the Filters card. Tick one region and click OK . Watch how the bars change. Then clear the filter so all regions are included again. Write it down Every time you filter, record it. A chart without its filters written down is easy to misread later. Save and reopen ¶ Choose File → Save As and save the workbook in your course folder, for example class01_first_view . Close Tableau, open it again and open your saved workbook. Check that the chart and your filter settings are still there. Part 4: Rows versus orders ¶ Open the Data Source page again and look at a few rows that share the same order_id . One row in this file is one order line : one product within an order. One order can have several lines. So the number of rows is not the number of orders. Quick check In the Data pane, Tableau lists a field named after the file with (Count) at the end. Drag it to the view. Is that counting rows or orders? Write your answer in one sentence. You will measure orders properly in Lesson 2 . Part 5: Independent work ¶ On a new sheet, build one more simple view on your own: Choose a different grouping: Region or Category . Show Sales for each group. Add a title that says what the chart shows and for which period. Write one sentence describing what the chart shows. Do not explain why yet. Part 6: Challenge ¶ A colleague says: "The biggest bar is the best segment, so we should invest there." In two or three sentences, explain why a bigger Sales bar alone does not tell us where to invest. What else would you want to see? Exit ticket ¶ Before you finish, write: Your one-sentence business question. What one row in order_lines.csv represents. One thing you are still unsure about. After the lesson ¶ Fix anything that did not work during setup. Read the Analytical workflow page. Start your evidence log (see Setup and practice ) with today's question, file name and filters.

docs.text: Lesson 2: Can we trust the sales table? ¶ Before comparing anything, find out exactly what the retail file contains: what a row is, which columns can be added up, and how to count orders correctly. Draft lesson The Tableau steps on this page have not yet been rehearsed on the course version of Tableau. Menu names may differ slightly on your computer. The business decision ¶ The retail head now asks: "Before you show me any chart, can I trust these numbers? How many orders did we actually have?" A wrong count at this stage spoils every later chart. Today is about building trust in the data. What you will be able to do ¶ By the end of this lesson you will be able to: State the grain of the file: what one row represents. Tell which columns are identifiers, categories, dates or amounts. Count orders correctly with a distinct count. Explain what the returns flag does and does not tell you. Check a small slice of data by hand. Record what you changed in a short preparation log . Evidence you keep: a grain statement, a short quality checklist, a preparation log and one checked order. Before you start ¶ Bring your saved Lesson 1 workbook and your evidence log. Keep the original order_lines.csv untouched. If you ever need to experiment, work on a copy. Part 1: Meet the data dictionary ¶ Every column has a job. Knowing that job tells you how to use it. Column What it is Can you add it up? row_id Unique number for each order line No, it is an identifier order_id Order identifier; repeats across that order's lines No, count it distinctly order_date , ship_date Calendar dates No order_month First day of the order's month, for monthly grouping No ship_mode Shipping service chosen No customer_id Fictitious customer identifier No segment Customer group: Consumer, Corporate or Home Office No, use it to group country_region , region Location labels No, use them to group category , sub_category Product groups No, use them to group product_id , product_name Product identifier and name No sales Sales reported for the line, in the file's own monetary units Yes quantity Number of items on the line Yes , but it counts items, not orders profit Profit reported for the line (can be negative) Yes discount Discount value as given in the source No, its exact definition is not documented returned_order_flag 1 if the order appears on the source's returns list, otherwise 0 Not on line rows (see Part 4) order_to_ship_days Days between order date and ship date No, not without care customer_analysis_eligible , customer_order_conflict Flags for a small data issue with customer IDs Used only for customer analysis later Scope of this file The file contains orders placed from 1 January 2023 to 31 December 2025 . A few orders placed late in 2025 shipped in early 2026; they are kept because the order date is what defines the period. Part 2: Find the grain ¶ Grain means: what does one row represent? Open your workbook and go to the Data Source page. Sort or scan the preview by order_id . Find an order that appears on more than one row . Compare those rows. What is the same? What is different? Write your grain statement Complete this sentence in your log: "One row in order_lines.csv represents one _ _ , identified by ____ ." Part 3: Count orders correctly ¶ Demonstration ¶ Your facilitator will show two numbers side by side: the number of rows (the field ending in (Count) ) the number of distinct orders Predict before you see them: will the two numbers be equal, or which will be larger? Guided practice ¶ On a new sheet, drag the (Count) field to the view. This counts rows. Drag Order Id into the view as well. Right-click it and choose Measure → Count (Distinct) . This counts orders. Put both numbers in a small table and label them clearly. Write one sentence explaining why they differ. A reusable calculation You can also create a calculated field named Orders with the formula: COUNTD([Order Id]) Use this whenever a chart needs a number of orders. Part 4: What the returns flag means ¶ returned_order_flag is 1 when an order appears on the source's returns list . Be careful with what it does not tell you: It has no return date, quantity or refund amount. A 0 means not on the list . It does not prove the order was never returned. The flag repeats on every line of a listed order. A common mistake Adding up returned_order_flag across lines counts lines of returned orders, not returned orders . To count returned orders, count distinct order_id values where the flag is 1. Part 5: Check one order by hand ¶ Pick one order with several lines. Filter the view to that single order_id . Show each line's sales and profit in a table. Add up the lines yourself on paper or in a spreadsheet. Compare with Tableau's total for that order. Do they match?
